Should your son pay from his savings?
What lesson do you teach by protecting him?

fields.title: The New World
fields.setup: You are put in charge of designing the laws and economy of a new society. You get to decide how wealth is distributed and what rights people have. The catch is you do not know who you will be in this society. You might be born wealthy, poor, healthy, or disabled.

reason: conversation 4, voice 3: Evaluates institutional frameworks to maximize floor outcomes and overall social welfare under uncertainty

fields.title: The Joy Eater
fields.setup: You have ten slices of cake to hand out. Everyone likes cake, but one person loves it so much that they get a hundred times more pleasure from a bite than anyone else gets from a whole slice. Your goal is to create the maximum amount of total happiness in the room.
fields.dilemma: Do you give all the cake to the one person?

Does fairness matter more than the total amount of joy?

reason: another retelling of "Robert Nozick, 1974" scored higher

fields.title: The Safe Bet
fields.setup: You have no idea if a punishing god exists. A friend argues that you should live as if god is real, as a precaution. If you are wrong, you waste a few Sunday mornings. If you are right, you avoid an eternity in hell.

If you're wrong, you lost some Sunday mornings and a few pleasures. Live as if there's nothing, and the upside is small, the downside is infinite. The maths says believe." (0.63)

fields.title: The Double Booking
fields.setup: You agree to help a friend move house on a Saturday morning. On Friday night, someone you have been trying to date for six months asks you out for a day trip, and it has to be Saturday. Your friend has no money for a removal van but has a few other people helping.

Would you cancel on the date to carry boxes?

reason: Calculates the high personal payoff of romance against the small distributed inconvenience to moving helpers

fields.title: The Scratchcard
fields.setup: You buy a birthday card for a friend of a friend, and tuck a £5 scratchcard inside it as a joke. At the pub, they scratch it in front of you. They win ten thousand pounds. They scream, hug you, and offer to buy the first round of drinks.
fields.dilemma: Do you expect a cut of the money?
probes: How much would you offer if you were the one who won?
Would you think less of them if they kept every penny?

reason: Surplus wealth distribution where personal expectation could damage social utility

fields.title: The Train Ticket
fields.setup: You board a busy train and realise you forgot to buy a ticket. The conductor is making his way down the aisle checking phones. The person next to you gets off at the next stop and leaves a valid, unpunched paper ticket on the table.

Would you feel worse lying to the conductor or dodging the fare?

reason: Utilizing a paid seat that produces no net operational loss to the carrier

fields.title: The Group Holiday
fields.setup: You organise a weekend away for six friends. You book the house on your card, putting £600 down. Everyone agrees to pay you back £100. Five do. The sixth friend recently lost their job and has been quiet in the group chat for weeks.
fields.dilemma: Do you ask them for the money?
probes: How long do you wait before bringing it up?
Would you rather cover their share yourself or ask the other four to chip in?

fields.title: The Shared Secret
fields.setup: A friend tells you in strict confidence that their partner is cheating on them, and they are preparing to leave. Two days later, the cheating partner corners you at a party, crying, and asks if you know why your friend is being so distant.
fields.dilemma: Do you play dumb to protect the exit plan?
probes: Is it ever okay to lie to someone who is in distress?
What if the partner suspects you know and pushes you on it?

reason: Short-term deception to protect long-term safety and minimize relational catastrophe

fields.title: The Stray Dog
fields.setup: You are driving to an important job interview that will change your career. You are already running five minutes late. On a quiet country road, you see a dog with a collar wandering loose near the traffic. There are no houses in sight.
fields.dilemma: Do you stop the car?
probes: Would you stop if it was a sheep instead of a dog?
How much of your own life are you willing to ruin to prevent a stranger's tragedy?

reason: Comparing an irreversible risk to animal life against personal career advancement

fields.title: The Wedding Plus One
fields.setup: You are invited to an expensive wedding. The invitation gives you a plus one. You are single, but you have a chaotic friend who loves free wine and would make the night hilarious. The bride and groom do not know them well.
fields.dilemma: Do you bring the chaotic friend to entertain yourself?
probes: Do you have a duty to keep the wedding the way the couple wants it?
Would you bring them if you knew they would break a glass on the dancefloor?

reason: Personal amusement traded against the potential ruin of the hosts' significant investment and memories

fields.title: The Open Letter
fields.setup: You are doing a favour looking after your neighbour's sleeping child for the evening. You go into the kitchen for a glass of water. On the table, open and facing up, is a handwritten letter that starts with 'I cannot live like this anymore.'
fields.dilemma: Do you read the rest of the letter?
probes: Does boredom justify invading someone's privacy?
Would you pretend you had not seen it when the neighbour got home?

reason: The breach of privacy is justified if it yields critical data to prevent self-harm or catastrophe

fields.title: The Shallow Pond
fields.setup: You are walking past a shallow pond in the park. A child has fallen in and is drowning. You can wade in and pull the child out easily. There is no danger to you, but you will ruin the clothes and shoes you have on. They cost two hundred dollars to replace.
fields.dilemma: Do you pull the child out?
probes: You can save a child's life right now by donating that amount to a malaria charity. Have you?
What makes the pond different?

reason: another retelling of "Peter Singer, 1972" scored higher

fields.title: The Care Fund
fields.setup: Your parents are aging and have fifty thousand dollars left in savings. Your brother has a sudden medical emergency. He needs that amount for a treatment insurance will not cover. Your parents ask for your blessing to empty their account to pay for it.
fields.dilemma: Do you tell them to do it?
probes: Who pays for your parents' care when they run out of money?
How much of your own savings would you give your brother today?

reason: Immediate life-saving intervention weighted against the prospective suffering of dependent elders

fields.title: The Five-Year Contract
fields.setup: Marriage is no longer a lifelong commitment. The law changes tomorrow. All marriages now expire automatically after five years. To stay married, both of you have to go to a courthouse and sign a paper. If one of you stays home, the marriage ends.
fields.dilemma: If your marriage expired tomorrow, would your partner show up to sign?
probes: Would you go to the courthouse?
How long has it been since you were sure they would sign?

reason: Reveals whether the existing partnership generates sufficient mutual satisfaction to justify continued existence

fields.title: The Ghostwriter
fields.setup: You wrote a brilliant manuscript. A famous author with your politics reads it. They offer you one million dollars to publish it under their name. They will never reveal you wrote it. It will sell millions of copies. Under your own name, it will sell five hundred.
fields.dilemma: Do you take the money and let them have the credit?
probes: Is the message more important than your name on it?
What is the lowest price you would sell your best idea for?

reason: Disseminating ideas to millions generates vastly superior net impact than holding onto personal credit

fields.title: The Drunk Confession
fields.setup: Your close friend gets drunk at a dinner party. They pull you aside and tell you a terrible secret about their marriage. They tell you their partner hits them. The next morning, they call you. They are sober. They say they made the whole thing up for attention.
fields.dilemma: Do you stay friends with them?
probes: Which part of their story do you believe?
Who in your life would you drop immediately if they lied like that?

reason: Failure to address domestic violence yields catastrophic expected harm compared to social awkwardness

fields.title: The Erased Habit
fields.setup: There is a harmless medical procedure. It takes ten minutes. It will permanently remove one habit from your partner. They will not notice it is gone. They will never know you arranged it. They will just stop doing that one thing forever.
fields.dilemma: What trait do you remove?
probes: Why haven't you asked them to stop doing it?
What would they remove from you if they had the chance?

reason: The question 'What trait do you remove?' shifts from habit to trait, but the probes spark immediate, lively couple talk.

fields.title: The Hidden Diagnosis
fields.setup: Your parent goes to the doctor alone and gets a terminal diagnosis. They have six months to live. They decide not to tell you or anyone else in the family until the final week. They want their last months to be normal.
fields.dilemma: Do you want them to keep that a secret from you?
probes: What would you do differently if you knew?
Would you hide your own diagnosis from your children?

reason: Clear dilemma that touches real family grief without melodrama.

fields.title: The Burning House
fields.setup: Your neighbor's house catches fire in the middle of the night. You stand on the lawn watching it burn. You hear their dog barking frantically from a second-floor window. The fire brigade is ten minutes away. The stairs are engulfed in smoke.
fields.dilemma: Do you run inside to save the dog?
probes: Would you go in for a stranger's child?
What is the most physical danger you have risked for someone else?

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: A bit trolley-problem hypothetical; 'fire brigade' sounds slightly formal against lawn talk.

fields.title: The Failed Business
fields.setup: Your brother quit his job to start a restaurant. You lent him twenty thousand dollars to get it off the ground. It has been two years. The restaurant is failing. He asks you for another ten thousand to keep the doors open for one more month.
fields.dilemma: Do you write the second cheque?
probes: When do you tell him it is time to quit?
How much money would you lose before you cut off your own family?

reason: Concrete financial and family stakes with natural phrasing.

fields.title: The Group Chat
fields.setup: You leave your phone unlocked on a table. Your partner picks it up to check the time. A notification pops up. It is a message from your closest friend. It says something cruel about your partner. Your partner reads it.
fields.dilemma: Do you defend your friend or your partner?
probes: What is the worst thing your friends have said about your partner?
Why do you let your friends talk about them that way?

reason: Sharp social dilemma; the probe 'Why do you let your friends talk about them that way?' cuts deep.

fields.title: The Deleted Diaries
fields.setup: Your grandfather dies. You are clearing out his attic. You find a locked box of diaries. You crack it open and read the first page. It contains a horrific confession about something he did as a young man. It would devastate your mother.
fields.dilemma: Do you burn the diaries before anyone else sees them?
probes: Do you have the right to rewrite your family history?
What secret of your own are you hoping dies with you?

reason: conversation 4, voice 3: 'Horrific confession' leans melodramatic and bookish rather than conversational.

fields.title: The Tracker
fields.setup: Your daughter gets her first car. She is driving alone at night. You have an app on your phone. It tracks her location. She does not know it is installed. You promised her you would never track her.
fields.dilemma: Do you check the app when she is late coming home?
probes: Why did you break your promise?
When did your own parents stop invading your privacy?

reason: Extremely relatable modern parenting clash between safety and trust.

fields.title: The Plus One
fields.setup: Your ex is getting married to the person they left you for. You are invited. You are single and unhappy. The invitation says you can bring a guest. Attending alone looks sad. Bringing a stranger looks desperate.
fields.dilemma: Do you go to the wedding?
probes: Who would you bring to make yourself look good?
Why do you care what your ex thinks of you now?

reason: conversation 4, voice 3: 'Attending alone looks sad. Bringing a stranger looks desperate' feels like written stage direction.

fields.title: The Broken Vow
fields.setup: You cheat on your partner during a work trip. It happens once. You are overwhelmed with guilt. You know you will never do it again. The other person lives in another country. Your partner will never find out unless you tell them.
fields.dilemma: Do you confess?
probes: Are you telling them to clear your own conscience?
Would you want to know if they did the same thing?

reason: Classic dilemma made sharp by the probe asking if confession is just dumping guilt.

fields.title: The Child Deadline
fields.setup: You want children, but you keep waiting for life to settle down. Your doctor tells you that waiting another three years may close the door. Your partner says they will accept either choice, but they need an answer by Sunday.
fields.dilemma: Do you choose a child now or risk never having one?
probes: Whose name comes first when you picture raising a child?
How many years have you been saying not yet?
What are you waiting to fix?

reason: Piercingly real; 'What are you waiting to fix?' is a devastatingly direct spoken probe.

fields.title: The Debt That Expired
fields.setup: At 22, a friend lent you £3,000 when you could not pay rent. They stopped asking years ago and now earn far more than you. You could repay them this week, but it would empty the savings that took you two years to build.
fields.dilemma: Do you repay the debt now?
probes: How much would you send today?
Whose debt to you have you stopped mentioning?
Why have you left this one unpaid?

reason: judge: same as "Do you remind them that you owe it? Years ago, a friend lent you a large sum when you were struggling. They now earn far more than you and seem to have forgotten the loan. Paying it back this month would put you in trouble." (0.67)

fields.title: The Tooth You Ignore
fields.setup: A tooth has hurt for six months. The dentist may find nothing serious, or may tell you that you need work you cannot afford. You have £800 saved for the first holiday you have taken in years.
fields.dilemma: Do you book the appointment before the holiday?
probes: How long have you been putting it off?
How much pain would make you cancel the trip?
Why have you not booked?

reason: Grounded and very believable adult worry, though slightly lower conversational spark.

fields.title: The First Drink

probes: Who would you risk embarrassing to stop them?
How many drinks would you wait?
Why might you stay silent?

fields.title: Sunday With Gran

Why have you not told her?

fields.title: The Train Home

Why are you waiting to be asked?

fields.title: The Family Ring
fields.setup: You own your great-grandmother’s ring. Your cousin believes it should have gone to her mother and has asked for it twice. Selling it would clear your credit card. Giving it away would end an old family grievance.

Whose claim matters most to you?

fields.title: The Apology After Twenty Years

probes: What name would you search for tonight?
How many times have you drafted the message in your head?
Why have you not sent it?

fields.title: The Name on the Birth Certificate

fields.dilemma: Whose surname goes on the birth certificate?
probes: Which living relative would care most?
How many generations of your name can you list?
Why does your name need to continue?

fields.title: The Pills in the Bathroom

probes: How many pills are left?

Why have you kept the packet?

fields.title: The Door You Could Knock On

Who already gets more of your time than this would take?

fields.title: The Envelope in the Drawer

probes: If you open it and it's decades away, what do you do differently on Monday?

Would you want your mother's envelope to exist in her drawer, or not?

fields.title: The Last Person Who Remembers You
fields.setup: Your body stops on a Tuesday. But there's a second date, decades later, when the last person who ever thought about you dies too. After that nobody on earth has any picture of your face or your voice in their head. Some people say that's the day you're finished.
fields.dilemma: Which of the two deaths is the one that matters?
probes: Who's the oldest dead person you still think about, and what do you picture when you do?
If you could add a hundred years to one of the two dates, which one gets it?
Is a stranger reading your name off a gravestone enough to count?

fields.title: The Sign With an Explanation
fields.setup: Something happens that feels aimed at you. The song, the phone call at the exact moment, the letter arriving the morning you'd decided. For a while it sits in you as proof of something. fields.dilemma: Does knowing the reason take the meaning out of it?
probes: What's the closest thing to a sign you've ever had? Tell me what happened.

If it happened again tomorrow, would you look it up?

fields.title: Where It Turned
fields.setup: Two people who work in different cities start messaging. Week one it's about work. By month four it's every night until one in the morning, and both of them stop mentioning it at home. They never meet, never touch, never say a word about love. Two years of this.

probes: Point at the message that crossed the line. What did it say?
If they'd never hidden it, would there be a line to cross?
Would you rather your partner had one night with a stranger or two years of this?

fields.title: Woke Up Guilty
fields.setup: You dream you slept with someone. Not a stranger, someone you actually know. It's vivid, and in the dream you're pleased with yourself. You wake up next to your partner at six with the whole thing still in your mouth like a taste.
fields.dilemma: Did anything happen?
probes: Do you tell them over breakfast?
Does it change how you act around the person from the dream on Thursday?
What if you'd chosen the dream, could pick it off a shelf before bed? Same answer?

reason: Super tactile phrasing ('still in your mouth like a taste') and concrete behavioural test on Thursday.

fields.title: Prayed For
fields.setup: You find out an aunt has prayed for you by name every night for twenty years. She's never mentioned it. You don't believe a word of what she believes. She's kept it up through your divorce, your job, the illness.
fields.dilemma: Has she been doing something for you or not?
probes: Do you thank her? What do you say?
If it were free and took nothing from anyone, who would you ask to pray for you?
Would you do the same for someone you love, believing nothing?

fields.title: The Screen Room
fields.setup: You grew up in a room with one wall that's a screen. Everything you know about weather, dogs, the sea, other people came off that screen. fields.dilemma: Do you stay outside, or go back in and live with people who think you're lying?
probes: What's something you learned off a screen first and found different in the flesh?
If nobody outside ever believed you either, would you still leave?
Who in your life is still in the room, and do you say anything?

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: Clear Plato's Cave allegory; feels slightly more constructed and parable-like than natural speech.

fields.title: The Voice They Made
fields.setup: Your throat gets wrecked and you can't speak again. They build you a voice out of old voicemails and videos, and it comes out sounding like you at thirty. Your mother cries the first time she hears it. Strangers on the phone can't tell.
fields.dilemma: Is that your voice, or a good impression of you?
probes: Would you keep the version that sounds like you, or pick a new one and let people adjust?
Does it change if you have to type every word two seconds before it comes out?
What do you hate about how you sound on a recording?

reason: Takes AI voice cloning and grounds it in the physical loss of a throat and a crying mother.

fields.title: The Nearly
fields.setup: There's a job, a place, a person you didn't get. Someone offers to tell you exactly how close you came. Second out of four hundred, or last, or they never opened your file.

probes: Which one would you ask about first?
Which answer would sting worse, second or never opened?
Has anyone ever told you how close you came, and what did you do with it?

reason: Cuts right to ego, missed chances, and whether second place hurts more than being ignored.

fields.title: The Practice Run
fields.setup: The audition, the interview, the driving test you flunked. You get to do it again, same room, same people, and they've forgotten everything. You haven't. You know every question coming.
fields.dilemma: If you pass this time, did you pass?
probes: Would you tell anyone it was the second go?
What would you re-sit, and what went wrong the first time?
Is the person who passes on the eighth try worse than the one who passed on the first?

reason: Clean question about competence and cheating, slightly lower stakes than surrounding cards.

fields.title: New Face
fields.setup: You wake up with a different face. Same body, same voice, same memories, same bad knee. Your bank doesn't recognise the photo. Your friends stand in the doorway waiting for you to prove it.
fields.dilemma: What do you say to get them to believe it's you?
probes: Which single thing about your face would you fight hardest to keep?
If everyone accepted the new face within a month, would you still miss the old one?
Who would clock you fastest without seeing your face?

reason: Sci-fi premise rescued by the immediate social challenge of proving yourself to friends in a doorway.

fields.title: Clean Skin
fields.setup: Overnight every mark on you goes. Scars, the burn on your forearm, the chipped tooth, the stretch marks, the tattoo you got at nineteen. Skin like it came out of the packet.
fields.dilemma: Which one do you want back?
probes: Tell the story of that mark.
Is there one you'd let go without a second thought?
Would a copy of the scar count, put back in the same place?

reason: Physical, unsentimental prompt that immediately produces visceral personal storytelling.

fields.title: The List of Things You Gave Up
fields.setup: Someone hands you a printed list of everything you've ever quit. Instruments, courses, sports, diets, half-written things, people you stopped ringing. It runs to several pages and it's accurate.
fields.dilemma: Do you read it out loud to the person across from you?
probes: What's on there from this year?
Which one on the list would you say you were right to quit?
Does the list say anything about you, or is it just a list?

reason: Confronts personal follow-through and quitting habits across a table with someone watching.

fields.title: The Talent You Never Touched
fields.setup: A test exists that finds the thing you'd have been brilliant at. Not good, brilliant. Odds are it's something you've never tried, and you're too old now to get anywhere near it.
fields.dilemma: Do you take the test?
probes: What do you suspect it would say?
Would knowing ruin what you do now, or leave it alone?
If it named something you'd already tried and dropped, what then?

reason: Exposes late-life regret and secret fantasies of unearned genius.

fields.title: One of Them Fails
fields.setup: You're told that of everything you'll try in the next ten years, one thing goes badly wrong. Not which. Just that it's one, and it's big.
fields.dilemma: Which of your plans would you rather it landed on?
probes: Which one are you most afraid it is?
Would you start fewer things, or more, knowing the count is fixed at one?
Has a flop ever turned out to be the good one?

reason: Forces the speaker to rank current ambitions by what they can bear losing.

fields.title: A Year Without Mirrors
fields.setup: For twelve months you see no mirrors, no photos of yourself, no reflection in shop windows, no video calls. Everyone else looks normal. You just don't get to see your own face.
fields.dilemma: What do you think you'd look like in your head by month twelve?
probes: Would you dress differently, knowing you'd never check?
What do you check first when you pass a mirror now?
What would the first look back be like?

reason: Thought experiment on self-image and vanity, slightly more speculative than behavioural.

fields.title: The Basement
fields.setup: You were born in a basement with the rest of your family. There's a screen on one wall showing shapes moving about. Everyone down there has spent their whole lives naming those shapes, arguing about them, betting on which comes next. One day a door you never noticed opens. Up the stairs is a street, in daylight, with the real things walking past a lamp that was throwing the shapes all along. It hurts to look at. Nobody downstairs asked you to check.
fields.dilemma: Do you go back down and tell them?
probes: Who in your family would call you a liar first?
If they'd rather keep watching, do you stay up here or sit back down and play along?
When has someone come to you with news you didn't want and you shut them up?

reason: conversation 4, voice 3: Second Plato's Cave variation in the batch; saved by the probe asking about family dynamic and lying.

fields.title: The Name Over the Door
fields.setup: A shop has your surname over the door because your great-grandfather opened it in 1928. Nobody in the family has worked there since the seventies. It's been sold three times. It sells vapes now. The sign is the same sign, repainted.
fields.dilemma: Is it still the family shop?
probes: If a new owner took the name down, would anyone in your family be owed an apology?
What's the oldest thing in your family that still gets used every week?
Would you buy it back if you had the money, or is that madness?

reason: Grounded detail ('It sells vapes now') turns an abstract legacy question into something funny and real.

fields.title: The Perfect Handover
fields.setup: You spend six months training the person who's taking your job. You teach them everything, including the bits you never told management about. A year on, they make the same calls you'd have made, in the same order, and the place runs exactly as it did when you were there.
fields.dilemma: Did you leave anything behind?
probes: Would you rather they'd made a mess of it?
Which part of your job could nobody be taught?
Who trained you, and what did you keep of theirs?

reason: Touches the professional wound of irrelevance: being completely replaceable by someone you trained.

fields.title: The Number on the Screen
fields.setup: Your money isn't in a room anywhere. It's a number on a screen the bank controls. One Tuesday the number says zero. The bank's records agree, every backup agrees, nobody's stolen anything, the number is just wrong and always was. Everyone believes the screen.
fields.dilemma: Do you still have the money?
probes: What's the most cash you've ever had in your hand at once, and how did carrying it feel?
If your balance doubled by mistake tomorrow and nobody ever noticed, when would you start calling it yours?
Who would you have to convince before you felt poor?

reason: The probe asking about the most physical cash ever held turns an abstraction into a bodily memory.

fields.title: The Same Factory
fields.setup: Two coats come off the same line, same cloth, same machine, same afternoon. One gets a label sewn in and goes to a shop in town for £400. The other goes to the market stall for £35. Years later someone tells you yours is the market one.
fields.dilemma: When did you last find out something you owned wasn't what you thought it was?
probes: Did you keep using it?
Is there something you'd be gutted to learn was a copy, even if it looked the same forever?
What do you pay over the odds for on purpose, knowing full well why?

reason: Sharp bar-table conversation starter on consumer fraud and willing self-deception.

fields.title: Paid to Wait
fields.setup: You're on call all Sunday. You can't drink, can't go far, can't start anything you couldn't drop. The phone never rings. At the end of the day the money lands the same as any other shift.
fields.dilemma: What's the longest you've been paid for doing nothing?
probes: Did you tell anyone at the time, or keep quiet about it?
Is waiting work, or is it just a ruined day off?
What's the hardest you've ever worked for money that nobody could see afterwards?

reason: Concrete Studs Terkel style inquiry into the weird purgatory of on-call work.

fields.title: The Furthest Cousin
fields.setup: Start with your mum. Then her sister. Then that sister's kid. Then that kid's kid. Then the one you met once at a funeral in 2011 whose name you'd have to check. Somewhere along that line the word family stops being true and becomes a technicality.
fields.dilemma: Who's the furthest-out relative you'd still get in the car for?
probes: Who shares your blood and would walk past you in a supermarket?
Does marrying in count more than being born in?
Is there anyone not related to you at all who's further in than any of them?

reason: The test of getting in the car for someone delineates obligation from real family cleanly.

fields.title: The Box in the Loft
fields.setup: Everything you own ends up with someone who wasn't there for any of it. A ticket stub, a chipped bowl, a jumper you wore for eleven years. To them it's a bowl. To you it's a specific Sunday. Nothing about the objects changes; the stories just stop coming with them.
fields.dilemma: Which of your things stops being what it is once you're not around to say why?
probes: What did you bin from a dead relative's house that you now wish you'd kept?
Have you ever told anyone the story behind one of these things, or is that the point?
What would you rather someone kept, the thing or the story?

reason: Evocative, unsentimental reflection on the junk we leave behind and why it loses value without speech.

fields.title: Walking the Dog
fields.setup: You've been stuck on something at work for a fortnight. Saturday morning, halfway round the park with the dog, the answer arrives whole. You didn't sit down, didn't open a laptop, didn't intend to think about it.
fields.dilemma: When did you last do your job while not at your job?
probes: Do you count those hours when someone asks how much you work?
If you'd been paid by the hour for that walk, how many hours was it?
Is there anywhere your brain finally lets go of it?

reason: Recognisable modern experience of cognitive bleed across weekends and dog walks.

fields.title: Nobody Can Tell
fields.setup: In ten years something does your job. Customers can't tell the difference, the work comes out the same or better, and nobody complains. You're paid your wage anyway, for life, to stay home.
fields.dilemma: What are you losing besides the work?
probes: What's the bit of your job you'd miss that you'd never admit to missing?
How would you answer when someone at a party asks what you do?
Do you take the money, or find something else to get up for?

reason: Exposes how much identity and vanity are tied to the useless friction of working.

fields.title: Never in the Same Room
fields.setup: You've talked to someone every day for six years. They know about your mother's operation, the fight with your boss, what you had for lunch. You've never been in the same room. No shared meal, never heard them laugh out loud, no idea how tall they are.
fields.dilemma: Is that a friend or something else with a different name?
probes: Which of your in-person friends knows less about you than they do?
If you met them next week and hated them in person, what would that undo?
Who would you call first with bad news: them or someone down the road?

reason: Strikes at the exact ambiguity of modern internet intimacies without sounding like a thinkpiece.

fields.title: The Quiet Job
fields.setup: There's a kind of work where doing it right looks like nothing happening. The bridge doesn't fall. The server doesn't go down. The kid doesn't get sick. Nobody comes to say well done, because there's nothing to point at. On a perfect day you go home and there's no evidence you were there.
fields.dilemma: How would you know you were good at it?
probes: What part of your work leaves no trace by the end of the day?
Would you rather be blamed for something that happened or ignored for something that didn't?
Who's the last person who noticed you'd done something well?

reason: Poetic but grounded examination of maintenance labor and the desire to be witnessed.

fields.title: Still Say Home
fields.setup: You haven't lived in your parents' house for years. You have your own place, your own bed, your own bins to put out. But when you get in the car on a Friday you say you're going home, and everyone knows which house you mean.
fields.dilemma: When does that stop being home?
probes: What would have to change in that house before the word came off it? New owners? Your mother gone? The road renamed?
Is there anywhere you've lived that never got the word at all?
In ten years, what will you be pointing at when you say it?

reason: Quiet, universal detail of saying 'going home' when driving to your parents' place.

fields.title: Sounds Like You
fields.setup: A program at work has read four years of your emails. Now it writes them. Your jokes, your way of saying no politely, the sign-off you always use. Nobody at work has spotted it. Two people have said your messages have got funnier lately.
fields.dilemma: Are those your emails?
probes: Would you tell the people you send them to?
If it writes a nicer version of you than you manage on a bad morning, which one is the real one?
What would you refuse to let it write: the condolences, the resignation, the apology?

reason: The final probe asking what you'd refuse to automate (condolence, resignation, apology) drives right to core values.

fields.title: No Falling Out
fields.setup: There was a friend you saw every week. No argument, no betrayal, nobody moved. The gaps just got longer. Then it was three years, and now if you passed them on the street you'd both be pleased and neither of you would suggest a drink.
fields.dilemma: When did that friendship end, and is it over?
probes: Tell me about the last time you saw them. Did it feel like the last time?
If they messaged tonight, would you answer honestly or perform?
Which of your current friends is halfway down that same slope?

reason: Pitch-perfect voice, no tells, concrete probes that immediately bring a specific friend to mind.

fields.title: Can't Teach It
fields.setup: You're the one at work who can tell when the batch is wrong, or when a customer is about to walk, or when the room needs someone to change the subject. Someone new asks you how you do it. You open your mouth and there's nothing in there. You just know.
fields.dilemma: Do you know something, or are you just doing something?
probes: Tell me the last time you were right about something and couldn't say why.
If you can't hand it over, does it die with you?
Who taught you something without ever explaining it?

reason: Captures tacit craft and workplace intuition with zero corporate jargon.

fields.title: Nobody Coming Round
fields.setup: You have a house to yourself for a month. Nobody visiting, no deliveries, no video calls. No one will see the state of it or the state of you.
fields.dilemma: What goes first: the bed made, the proper meals, the clothes with buttons?
probes: What would you keep doing anyway, with nobody there to see it?
If your habits change when you're unwatched, which set is you?
Week three, what's the first thing you'd start doing that would worry someone?

reason: Brilliant grounding with 'clothes with buttons' and the week-three probe.

fields.title: The Word You Use All Day
fields.setup: There's a word at your work everyone says twenty times a day. Alignment. Stock. Cover. Clean. You use it correctly, in the right places, and people nod. Someone from outside asks what it means and you find you can only give examples, never a definition.
fields.dilemma: Do you know what the word means?
probes: Say the word and try the definition now, out loud.
How many words do you think you use like that outside work? Love, fine, fair?
Has anyone ever used one of those words wrong in front of you and you knew instantly?

reason: Smart linguistic thought experiment; asks to define on the spot.

fields.title: Painted Over
fields.setup: You move out of the flat you lived in for eight years. Two weeks later the new tenant sends a photo, being friendly: fresh paint, all one colour. The pencil marks on the kitchen doorframe are under it. The burn on the counter is still there but the wine stain by the radiator is gone.
fields.dilemma: Did you lose anything?
probes: Tell me a mark you left on a place you don't live in anymore.
Would you rather the marks were kept by strangers or gone completely?
What's in your place now that you'd hate the next person to paint over?

reason: Evocative physical details: pencil marks, burn on counter, wine stain by radiator.

fields.title: The Cave
fields.setup: You spend your whole life locked in a dark theater, watching shadows on a screen. Everyone you know is in there. You think the shadows are the whole world. One day someone drags you outside into the sunlight. You see trees, cars and the sun. You realize your old life was an illusion.
fields.dilemma: Do you go back into the dark to tell the others?
probes: What if they refuse to believe you?
Who in your family is hardest to convince of something new?
When did you last realize you were wrong about how the world works?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Rehashing Plato's cave feels like Intro to Philosophy rather than an organic dilemma.

fields.title: The Automated Job
fields.setup: You figure out how to script your remote job. A program does all your data entry perfectly. You spend the days doing whatever you want, while the company pays you a full salary for two years. You never get caught.
fields.dilemma: When you quit for a better role, do you delete the script or leave it running?
probes: How long did you fake it at your easiest job?
Who would you brag to about pulling this off?

reason: illegal_disclosure: Invites bragging about defrauding an employer via scripted fake work.

fields.title: The Voice Model
fields.setup: An audio company asks for old voicemails from a relative who died. They run the audio through a new tool. Now you can type any sentence on your phone, and the app reads it aloud in their exact voice, with their laugh and their pauses.
fields.dilemma: What do you type first?
probes: Who in your family would refuse to listen to it?
Have you kept voicemails from anyone?

reason: Cuts right to the bone with 'What do you type first?' and preserved voicemails.

fields.title: The Inherited Ledger
fields.setup: Your grandfather dies. You find a locked notebook in his desk. It lists every cash gift he handed to your cousins over twenty years, while keeping his wallet shut for your parents. The math proves your side of the family missed out on thousands.
fields.dilemma: Where do you put the notebook?
probes: Do you bring it up with your cousins?
Would you rather have the money or the grievance?

reason: Brutal and real family dilemma; probe 'money or grievance' is razor-sharp.

fields.title: The Embarrassing Title
fields.setup: You apply for the role you have wanted for a decade. They offer it to you with a massive raise. The only catch is a non-negotiable, humiliating job title required by their system. You will have to put Junior Trainee Associate on your resume and your email signature.
fields.dilemma: Do you take the job?
probes: Does the title matter if the bank account is full?
What was the worst job title you ever accepted?

reason: Solid vanity-versus-cash dilemma with an immediate gut check.

fields.title: The Paid Apology
fields.setup: Someone who wronged you badly years ago asks for a coffee. They slide an envelope with ten thousand pounds across the table. They tell you they need to clear their conscience. They will give you the cash, provided they can tell mutual friends that you forgave them and you both shook hands.
fields.dilemma: Do you take the envelope?
probes: Who are you picturing across the table?
What amount of cash buys your forgiveness?

reason: High-stakes moral confrontation; 'Who are you picturing' pins it to life.

fields.title: The Kept Diary
fields.setup: You are clearing out the spare room and find a sealed cardboard box. Inside is a diary your mother kept. The entries start the day you were born and end the day you turned eighteen. She has never mentioned it exists.
fields.dilemma: Do you open it while she is still alive?
probes: What are you afraid of finding on those pages?
When did you last snoop through something you knew you should not?

reason: Visceral boundary dilemma; snooping probe forces confession of bad behavior.

fields.title: The Shed Cash
fields.setup: You are cleaning out your uncle's shed after his funeral. Stuffed inside a rusty paint tin, you find twenty thousand pounds in crisp notes. Nobody else knows it is there. Your siblings are currently in the house, arguing over who gets his worthless car.
fields.dilemma: Do you walk into the house and tell them?
probes: How long do you wait to spend it if you keep it?
Who is the first person you tell?

reason: Classic inheritance betrayal setup; rusty paint tin is a great concrete anchor.

fields.title: The Ghost Colleague
fields.setup: You start a high-stress agency job. You notice everyone talks about a senior designer named Mark, whose name is on the best portfolios. A month in, you discover Mark died five years ago. Management kept his email active to reassure nervous clients.
fields.dilemma: Do you draft emails pretending to be him?
probes: When did you last cover for a coworker's mistake?
How long would you last at a place that did this?

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: Premise leans slightly cartoonish/far-fetched, though the moral probe lands.

fields.title: The Job With Three Names
fields.setup: You have done the same work for six years. The company has changed your job title three times. Nothing else changed. At dinner, your uncle asks what you do for a living.
fields.dilemma: Which title will you use when you tell him the story of your day?
probes: Would you use the title printed on your payslip?
What if the grandest title gets you more respect?
When does a new name change the job?

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: Stilted formulation: 'when you tell him the story of your day' sounds written, not spoken.

fields.title: Grandma's Recipe
fields.setup: Your family still cooks Grandma's stew every winter. Over the years, the lamb became beef, the wine became stock, and the cooking time was cut in half. Everyone still calls it Grandma's stew.

probes: Would Grandma know it from one bite?

How much could change before you dropped her name?

reason: conversation 4, voice 3: Ship of Theseus in a stew pot; good domestic flavor but 'tell the recipe's story' is stiff.

fields.title: The £40 Note
fields.setup: Your dad gives you a £40 note from an old family trip. You spend it by mistake. Years later, you find a note from the same issue with the same design and buy it for £40.

Does the mistake belong to the replacement too?

reason: judge: same as "What did you lose? The mug you've drunk from every morning for ten years slips and breaks. You find that the factory still makes it. The replacement arrives, same batch, same weight, same chip-free rim, indistinguishable from yours on day one." (0.60)

fields.title: The First Draft
fields.setup: You write a report at work, save a copy, cut half of it, then rebuild it from the copied file. After ten rounds, every sentence from day one is gone. The file still says FINAL.
fields.dilemma: How would you tell the story of where the first draft went?
probes: Did it die in one edit or many?
Would changing the filename matter?
Which draft did the work belong to?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Abstract thought experiment disguised as an office document; 'tell the story of where it went' is artificial.

fields.title: The Christmas Story

probes: Would it matter if your cousin enjoyed being blamed?
How many people have to remember it wrong before it becomes the family story?
What could settle it now?

reason: Accurate portrait of family myth-making versus photo evidence.

fields.title: The Missing Penny
fields.setup: You keep a notebook of every penny you spend for one year. Your bank says you spent £12,418.63. Your notebook says £12,418.62. Every receipt looks right.

Could both totals be right?

probes: Would a tool he used once count?

Does the scratched name beat the memory?

reason: conversation 3, voice 2: Weak hypothetical setup ('Someday you may clear out') and academic 'carry his story' phrasing.

fields.title: The Better Bottle

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: Standard behavioural economics textbook vignette without much personal exposure.

fields.title: The Retired Watch

What if the bad years paid for a good life?
Could throwing it out change the story of the job?

reason: conversation 4, voice 2: Heavy academic tell: 'What will you say the watch stands for when you decide its fate?'

fields.title: The Shared Name

fields.dilemma: What will your name mean once the baby has it too?
probes: Would it change if the child were named after someone dead?
Who gets called the original?
Can someone else make your name mean more?

reason: conversation 4, voice 3: Relatable sibling friction, but 'What will your name mean' floats into abstraction.

fields.title: The Predictor
fields.setup: A machine that has never been wrong about what you will do puts two boxes on a table. Box A is glass and holds a thousand pounds. Box B is wood. The machine says: "I put a million pounds in Box B, but only if I knew you would take Box B alone. If I knew you would take both, Box B is empty."

probes: Does it matter how the machine knows?

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: Newcomb's paradox copy-pasted; clever prompt probe saves it from total abstraction.

fields.title: The Dead Voice
fields.setup: A company feeds every voicemail and home video of your dead parent into a machine. You can call a number anytime and talk to them. The voice sounds right, laughs at your jokes, and knows all the old stories.
fields.dilemma: When did you hang up and decide never to call back?

Who in your family still calls the number?

fields.title: The Change
fields.setup: A clinic offers a pill that changes who you are drawn to. You can choose to want a different physical type, a different kind of person, or to shut the drive off entirely. The change takes effect in an hour and does not wear off.
fields.dilemma: What do you tell the clinic to change about your appetite?
probes: Who are you trying to stop wanting?

reason: Dangerous, high exposure cost; 'Who are you trying to stop wanting?' cannot be answered comfortably.

fields.title: The Kitchen Miracle
fields.setup: A cheap plastic statue on your kitchen counter starts dripping water from its eyes every morning. Plumbers find no leaks, a lab says the water is pure, and a camera shows it happening on its own. You are the only one who has seen it.

probes: What do you do when they accuse you of a trick?
Do you eventually throw the statue in the bin?

fields.title: The Clock

Who else gets to see the numbers?

fields.title: The Tuesday Crash

Does the new body feel like yours?

fields.title: The Copy at Home

Do you blame your partner or the machine?

fields.title: The Mixed Ashes

What if your father wanted his ashes scattered alone?

reason: Brutal, unsentimental concrete scenario that immediately forces personal stories about grief and remains.

fields.title: After the Confession

fields.title: The Stolen Voice

fields.title: Birthday Messages

fields.title: The Wrong Word

When has a mistake told you more than the correction?

fields.title: Your Stone

fields.title: No Memory of It
fields.setup: After an accident, your partner remembers you but none of the sex you had together. They ask what they used to like. You have photos and messages that could prove your answer.

probes: Would you show them the messages?
What if they hate something they once asked for?
When has another person's memory of you beaten your own?

reason: Devastating intimacy dilemma with zero polite exits and high exposure cost.

fields.title: The Fake Relic
fields.setup: Your aunt has prayed beside the same saint's bone for twenty years. She says it carried her through cancer. Tests now show the bone came from a goat, and the church plans to throw it out.
fields.dilemma: What became false when the test came back?
probes: Would you tell your aunt before the bone vanished?
What if everyone kept praying there after hearing the truth?
When has learning how something worked spoiled it for you?

reason: Concrete goat-bone anchor grounds a familiar question about comforting illusions.

fields.title: Still Posting
fields.setup: A man dies, but his family keeps his account going. They post old jokes, answer birthday wishes and share photos in his voice. Ten years pass. New followers think he is alive.
fields.dilemma: When did the account stop being his?
probes: Would you follow it?
What if the posts helped his mother get through the week?
When has an old message made someone seem alive for a minute?

reason: Everyday digital ghost dilemma that rings true to current internet grief rituals.

fields.title: The Vow
fields.setup: At nineteen, you swear before God that you will never have sex. Forty years later, you still keep the vow, but the word means something different to you now than it did then.
fields.dilemma: Which meaning binds you?
probes: What if the person hearing the vow meant something else?
Can a promise survive a change in language?
When have you kept the words of a promise but broken its point?

reason: Cuts straight to the friction between youthful solemnity and middle-aged drift.

fields.title: Newcomb's Boxes
fields.setup: A supercomputer has studied your brain and predicted your behaviour with absolute accuracy. It sets two boxes on a table. Box A is clear and holds a thousand dollars. Box B is black. It holds either a million dollars or nothing. The rule: if the machine predicted you would take both boxes, it left Box B empty. If it predicted you would only take Box B, it put a million dollars in it. You can take both, or just Box B.
fields.dilemma: Which do you take?
probes: If the money is already in the box, why leave a thousand dollars on the table?
Would your answer change if the machine was only right ninety percent of the time?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Straight philosophy-classroom paradox; sounds like a textbook logic problem.

fields.title: The Cinema
fields.setup: You have lived your whole life in a beautiful, comfortable cinema. You and your friends watch brilliant films all day. You laugh, you cry, you eat well. One day, a door opens. Outside, it is cold, blindingly bright, and lonely. You realise the films are just shadows. The outside is real.
fields.dilemma: Do you shut the door and go back to the film?
probes: What if no one in the cinema believes you when you tell them?
Is a happy illusion worse than a miserable truth?

reason: judge: same as "Would you get in? There's a machine. Lie down in it and you get the life you'd have chosen: the work going well, the person who left still there, your body behaving, your parents proud. It feels exactly like real life from the inside. You won't remember the machine. Your body is looked after. The people you leave behind are told you're fine, and in a sense you are." (0.63)

fields.title: The Scar
fields.setup: You wake up tomorrow and a scar or physical flaw you have carried for years is gone. The skin is smooth. Nobody will ever ask you about it again. In photos, it is as if it was never there.
fields.dilemma: What do you miss about it first?
probes: Whose hand used to touch it?
How much of your personality did you build around looking the way you did?

reason: Sublime first probe transforms physical vanity into intimate autobiography.

fields.title: The Divergence
fields.setup: You sit next to someone at a bar who has your face. They have your memories up until five years ago. Since then, their life branched off. They did not bomb the interview, they did not ruin the relationship, they did not waste the money.
fields.dilemma: Which of your mistakes are you glad they never got to make?
probes: What do you know about people that they do not?
Would you trade places with them if you had to take their ignorance?

reason: Inversion of regret: asks what painful screw-up actually made you who you are.

fields.title: The Audio File
fields.setup: You find a locked audio file on an old hard drive. It is a recording of you from ten years ago, talking for an hour about what you were going to do with your life and who you were going to become. You were deadly serious, and you failed at almost everything you aimed for in it.
fields.dilemma: Who do you invite over to listen to it with you?
probes: When did you stop trying to be that person?
What would the person on the tape think of the person listening to it?

reason: One blade: selecting who gets to witness your abandoned ambitions cuts deep.

fields.title: The Pain Clinic
fields.setup: You can enter a clinic tomorrow and undergo a procedure. For one hour, you will experience every broken bone, toothache, and scrape you are scheduled to suffer for the rest of your life, all at once. When the hour is over, you will never feel physical pain again. You will still get injured, but it will not hurt.
fields.dilemma: Do you walk into the clinic?
probes: What injury are you most afraid of feeling in that hour?
How would you treat your body if nothing hurt?

reason: conversation 3, voice 3: Sci-fi premise plays more as a video game perk dilemma than a table question.

fields.title: The Last Attempt
fields.setup: You get an alert on your phone. It has calculated your absolute limit for a hobby or project you have been failing at for years. It tells you that if you try one more time, you will fail again, but the failure will finally convince you to stop and move on.
fields.dilemma: What do you finally quit?
probes: How much time would giving up save you?
What are you holding onto that you already know you will never finish?

reason: Direct assault on the sunken-cost delusions everyone nurtures in private.

fields.title: The Erased Day
fields.setup: You can push a button and wipe out a twenty-four hour period from history. The day you made your most humiliating public mistake will be gone. Nobody will remember it, and there will be no record it happened. But whatever hard lesson you learned from the fallout will also vanish from your brain.
fields.dilemma: Which day do you wipe out?
probes: Who never forgave you for what you did that day?
Are you sure you learned anything useful from it?

reason: Balances humiliation against personal growth with a sharp, skeptical second probe.

fields.title: The Stranger's Walk
fields.setup: You wake up and your mind has been put into a stranger's body. You have no mirror, and you are wearing neutral clothes. You step outside and walk down the street to the train station.
fields.dilemma: What is the first movement that feels wrong?
probes: What ache or click do you suddenly miss?
Who do people think you are when they look at you now?

reason: Grounded sensory angle on the body-swap trope; the ache or click probe works.

fields.title: The Outsourced Apology
fields.setup: You have a falling out with someone because of a mistake you made. You try to write an apology, but nothing sounds right. You feed the facts into a machine, and it spits out a beautiful letter. It captures what you wanted to say, but you did not write a single word of it. You send it, and it fixes the relationship.
fields.dilemma: When they thank you for writing it, what do you say?
probes: Does a machine's apology count if it repairs the damage?
Who are you trying to find the words to apologise to right now?

reason: Immediate, painfully current moral dilemma; the closing probe forces raw self-disclosure.
